title: Energy and Fossil Fuels
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the fuels that power modern life, the geopolitics they create, and the difficult transition to clean energy -- including Norway's own oil paradox.
competenceGoals: analyze the role of energy production in global politics and economics, with a focus on the transition from fossil fuels to renewable sources
discuss how energy policy affects different communities and nations, including issues of inequality and development

content.content:
## What powers your world

Every factory, vehicle, hospital, smartphone and heated building depends on a steady supply of energy. For over a century, that supply has been dominated by three fossil fuels -- coal, oil and natural gas -- which together still account for roughly 80 percent of global energy consumption. Modern civilisation, quite literally, runs on them.

The consequences are now impossible to ignore, and a fair account holds two truths at once. On one hand, fossil fuel combustion is the single largest source of the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change; it pollutes city air, causing millions of premature deaths a year; and competition for these resources has shaped and distorted international relations, fuelling wars and concentrating enormous wealth. On the other hand, fossil fuels powered the Industrial Revolution, lifted billions out of poverty, and enabled the modern standard of living much of the world enjoys. The challenge of this century is to move away from them without destroying the progress they made possible -- and to do so fast enough to avoid catastrophic warming.

## The fuels and the power they create

**Fossil fuels** are energy sources formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years; the three main ones are coal, oil and natural gas. They share defining characteristics. They are *non-renewable* -- once burned, they cannot be replaced on any human timescale. They are *carbon-intensive* -- burning them releases CO2, the primary greenhouse gas. They are *energy-dense*, packing a great deal of energy per unit, which is why they have been so economically valuable. And they are *unevenly distributed*, with large reserves concentrated in a relatively small number of countries, creating geopolitical power imbalances. Roughly, oil supplies about 31 percent of global energy, coal 27 percent, natural gas 24 percent, renewables including hydro about 13 percent, and nuclear about 5 percent. Key producers include Saudi Arabia, the US and Russia for oil; China, India and Indonesia for coal; and the US, Russia, Iran and Qatar for natural gas.

Norway offers a striking case study in the contradictions all this creates -- what might be called its oil paradox. Norway is often held up as an environmental leader: it has the world's highest rate of electric-vehicle adoption, generates nearly all its domestic electricity from hydropower, and has ambitious emission targets. Yet it is also one of the world's largest exporters of oil and natural gas, and its enormous wealth -- a sovereign fund exceeding 1.5 trillion dollars -- was built almost entirely on fossil fuel extraction. The country continues to issue new exploration licences, and although Norwegian producers argue their output is "cleaner," most emissions come from *burning* the fuel, not extracting it. In effect, Norway exports emissions: the oil and gas it sells generate roughly ten times more CO2 abroad than its entire domestic output. Supporters argue Norwegian gas can be a "bridge fuel" and that halting production abruptly would harm both Norway's economy and global energy security; critics call the position hypocritical. Environmental organisations have even sued the government over Arctic drilling licences. The paradox is not unique to Norway -- it mirrors the global dilemma.

questions.solution: Coal, oil and natural gas together still account for roughly 80 percent of global energy consumption.

questions.task: Which characteristic makes fossil fuels a source of geopolitical power imbalances?

questions.solution: Fossil fuels are unevenly distributed, with large reserves concentrated in a relatively small number of countries, creating geopolitical power imbalances.

content.content:
## The transition to clean energy -- and making it just

The response to all this is the **energy transition**: the large-scale shift from fossil-fuel-based energy systems to renewable and low-carbon sources, driven mainly by the need to cut emissions and limit climate change. It has several key elements. *Renewable energy expansion* means rapid growth of solar, wind and other sources to replace coal, oil and gas in electricity generation. *Electrification* means shifting transport, heating and industry from direct fossil-fuel use to electricity that can be generated cleanly. *Energy efficiency* means reducing the energy needed to power buildings, vehicles and industry. *Energy storage* means developing batteries and other technologies to handle the intermittent nature of solar and wind. And *phase-out* means gradually reducing and eventually eliminating fossil fuel extraction and use.

The transition faces enormous challenges, which is why a realistic account matters. Fossil fuels are deeply embedded in the global economy, with millions of jobs depending on them. Many developing nations lack the capital to invest in renewable infrastructure. Powerful fossil fuel companies and petrostates resist changes that threaten their interests. Energy storage and grid infrastructure must be massively expanded. And crucially, the transition must be *just* -- it should not disproportionately harm the workers and communities that depend on fossil fuel industries, nor should it deny developing nations the chance to grow. The central question, in the end, is not *whether* the energy transition will happen, since the science makes clear it must, but whether it will happen fast enough to prevent the worst warming, and whether it will be managed fairly for workers, communities and developing countries alike.

content.content:
## In short

Fossil fuels -- coal, oil and gas -- still supply about 80 percent of global energy, having powered modern civilisation while becoming the chief driver of climate change. They are non-renewable, carbon-intensive, energy-dense and unevenly distributed, creating geopolitical power imbalances. Norway's oil paradox -- branding itself a climate leader while exporting vast quantities of oil and gas -- captures the contradictions many nations face, with fair arguments on both sides. The energy transition involves expanding renewables, electrifying transport and heating, improving efficiency, developing storage and phasing out fossil fuels, but it faces deep challenges of economic dependency, investment and resistance. The transition must happen; the real questions are whether it will be fast enough and just enough for everyone affected.
